_note: swarf material palette. STUDENT-SAFE STARTING VALUES, not optimal ones — every entry is slow, shallow and survivable, and every one can be pushed once you know what the cut sounds like. Feeds and speeds assume HSS tooling, which is the limiting factor: HSS runs at roughly a third the cutting speed of the coated carbide in Langmuir's MR-1 chart, so RPM drops as the tool gets bigger rather than sitting at the machine's ceiling.
_cut: Each material carries one `cut` record and every tool's numbers are derived from it at apply time (window.__swarfDerive in swarf-material.js): rpm = vc x 1000 / (pi x D) clamped to the device's spindleMin..spindleMax; feed = rpm x flutes x chip x D (chip is chip load per mm of tool diameter, so the chip scales with the tool); plunge = 0.35 x feed, capped at the device's feedMaxZ and the process camFastFeedZ; stepdown = down x D, capped at downMax mm when set; stepover is a fraction of D. Device limits live in src/kiri/dev/cam/*.json. With carbide instead of HSS, vc can roughly triple.
_tooling: HSS, 2-flute for everything except mild steel, which assumes 4-flute. The tool library has no flute-count field, so nothing adapts automatically — running a 4-flute where 2 is assumed halves the chip load (safe, though it can rub in aluminum); running a 2-flute where 4 is assumed doubles it.
_units: vc m/min · chip mm per tooth per mm of diameter · down fraction of diameter · downMax mm · stepover fraction of diameter · ramp angle degrees. Derived: feed and plunge mm/min, spindle rpm, stepdown mm.
_ramp: ramp.angle drives camEaseAngle, ramp.ease drives camEaseDown — the tool walks down into the cut instead of drilling in on a flute that may not cut at center. 1.8 degrees is the MR-1 chart's helical-ramp figure and is used for the metals. Softer materials ramp steeper so the entry move stays short.
_rules: Invariants held over every tool in the default library on both devices, checked by tools/check_materials.mjs through the same derive function the app runs: plunge is 30-40% of feed unless the Z ceiling capped it; stepdown stays under half the tool diameter; spindle and feed inside the device limits; stepover in (0, 0.5]; feed never falls as the tool grows while the spindle holds steady.

materials.name: aluminum 6061
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. cutting speed 60 m/min, so RPM drops as the tool gets bigger — a 1/4 endmill at 8000 would burn its corners off. chips should curl, not powder.

materials.name: brass
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute, cutting speed 45 m/min. brass grabs a dull or rake-heavy tool and climbs the work — sharp cutter, light cut, climb direction.

materials.name: mild steel
materials.note: HSS, 4-flute, cutting speed 20 m/min. slow and shallow — this is the edge of what HSS will do. if the cut squeals or the tool discolors, stop. carbide is a different conversation.

materials.name: acrylic
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute — a single- or O-flute is better if you have one. cast PMMA. if the chip welds back into the cut, feed FASTER: melting comes from too little chip, not too much.

materials.name: polycarbonate
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. Lexan and similar — gummier than acrylic, it strings rather than chips. same rule: if it melts, feed faster.

materials.name: HDPE / Delrin
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. machining plastics — HDPE, UHMW, acetal. the most forgiving thing here after wax. HDPE springs back after the cut, so a finish pass measures undersized.

materials.name: MDF
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. abrasive — it dulls a cutter faster than hardwood does, and a dull cutter burns. dust extraction and a mask, always.

materials.name: hard wood
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. oak, maple, walnut, cherry. plywood cuts about the same, but the glue lines dull a cutter faster. dust mask required.

materials.name: machining wax
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. the safe rehearsal stock — cuts like butter and re-melts into a fresh block. prove a program here before cutting metal.

materials.name: foam
materials.note: HSS, 2-flute. rigid PU, EPS, blue/pink insulation. the risk is tool deflection on a long reach, not the cut.
